question: A 72-year-old man with longstanding history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset numbness. On your neurological exam, you note that he has loss of sensation on the left side of his face, arm, and leg. His motor strength exam is normal, as are his cranial nerves. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his presentation?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Hypertension and diabetes mellitus -> increased risk of stroke -> sudden-onset numbness -> possible stroke etiology -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Loss of sensation on the left side of the face, arm, and leg -> involvement of the right side of the brain -> likely cerebral artery stroke -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Normal motor strength exam and cranial nerves -> focal sensory deficit -> suggestive of a thalamic stroke -> 70%
analysis: Given the sudden-onset numbness affecting the left side of the face, arm, and leg, with normal motor strength and cranial nerves, the most likely explanation for his presentation is a thalamic stroke. Thalamic strokes can result in sensory deficits without significant motor weakness.
